follow_up_activities.title: Model Flink's streaming dataflow

content.heading: Sources, operators, sinks, and event time
content.body: A Flink job is a dataflow of sources, transformations, and sinks over unbounded streams. Event time (when an event happened) differs from processing time (when Flink observes it); most correct pipelines reason in event time.
key_points: A job is a directed dataflow of operators.
Event time is carried by the records, not the wall clock.
Processing time is simpler but non-deterministic under delay.

follow_up_activities.title: Trace an event-time pipeline

content.heading: Following a record through a Flink job
content.prompt: A click-stream is aggregated per user.
steps: Ingest records from a source with event timestamps.
Key the stream by user id.
Aggregate per key and emit to a sink.
content.reflection: What should happen to a record that arrives late?

follow_up_activities.title: Keyed state and checkpoints

content.heading: How Flink recovers
content.body: Operators keep keyed state; periodic checkpoints snapshot that state consistently, so a failed job can restart from the last checkpoint without losing or double-counting data.
key_points: State is scoped per key.
Checkpoints are consistent snapshots.
Recovery restores state and rewinds the source.

follow_up_activities.title: Check your recovery model

content.context: A Flink job crashes after processing half of a window.
content.prompt: What lets the job resume correctly?

options.label: Restore keyed state from the last checkpoint and rewind the source
Restart from scratch and reprocess everything from the beginning

follow_up_activities.title: Windows and watermarks

content.heading: Grouping unbounded streams
content.body: Windows slice an unbounded stream into finite chunks (tumbling, sliding, session). Watermarks signal that event time has advanced, so a window can close even though a few late records may still trickle in.
key_points: Windows bound an infinite stream.
Watermarks estimate event-time progress.
A lateness policy decides what to do with stragglers.

follow_up_activities.title: Choose a window and watermark

content.heading: A one-minute tumbling count
content.prompt: Count events per user per minute.
steps: Assign timestamps and a bounded-out-of-orderness watermark.
Apply a one-minute tumbling window keyed by user.
Emit the count when the watermark passes the window end.
content.reflection: How would a larger allowed lateness change the result?

follow_up_activities.title: Position, velocity, and acceleration

content.heading: Describing motion
content.body: Kinematics describes how objects move without asking why. Position tells you where an object is; velocity is how fast position changes; acceleration is how fast velocity changes. For constant acceleration, v = v0 + a*t.
key_points: Velocity is the rate of change of position.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
Constant acceleration gives linear velocity in time.

follow_up_activities.title: Newton's three laws

content.heading: Force and motion
content.body: Newton's laws connect force to motion: an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts (1st); net force equals mass times acceleration, F = m*a (2nd); forces come in equal and opposite pairs (3rd).
key_points: No net force means constant velocity.
F = m*a relates net force to acceleration.
Forces act in pairs between two bodies.

follow_up_activities.title: Work a force problem

content.heading: Acceleration from a net force
content.prompt: A 2 kg cart feels a net force of 6 N.
steps: Identify the net force (6 N) and mass (2 kg).
Apply F = m*a, so a = F / m.
Compute a = 6 / 2 = 3 m/s^2.
content.reflection: What happens to the acceleration if the mass doubles?

follow_up_activities.title: Work and energy

content.heading: Conservation of energy
content.body: Work transfers energy; kinetic energy is energy of motion (1/2 m v^2) and potential energy is stored (e.g. m*g*h). In an isolated system without friction, total mechanical energy is conserved.
key_points: Work is force applied over a distance.
Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed.
Total mechanical energy is conserved without losses.

follow_up_activities.title: Solve an energy problem

content.heading: Speed at the bottom of a ramp
content.prompt: A block slides from rest down a frictionless 1.8 m height.
steps: Set potential energy at the top equal to kinetic energy at the bottom.
m*g*h = 1/2 m v^2, so v = sqrt(2*g*h).
Compute v = sqrt(2 * 9.8 * 1.8) ~= 5.9 m/s.
content.reflection: How would friction change the result?
